title: Topic Analysis Incorporating Expert Knowledge: An Application to Science Analysis
summary: Topic models are great at finding patterns in documents, but they are rarely used outside research because they're too complex and do not fit into real workflows. This thesis tackles the "industrialization" of topic models—making them actually useful for policymakers and analysts who need to make sense of massive document collections. By putting domain experts at the center of the process, we show how to transform research algorithms into production tools that people can actually use for decision-making.

title: Topic models for decision-support systems. Part I: Training, representation and exploitation of topic models
summary: Policymakers need to analyze massive science and technology datasets to make informed decisions, but topic models are hard to tune and their outputs do not always match what experts need. We built TASE, a platform that lets experts guide topic model training, curation and evaluation and then deploy those models at scale for semantic search and decision support. We show it works on two real-world policy scenarios.

title: ProxAnn: Use-Oriented Evaluations of Topic Models and Document Clustering
summary: Topic models are tools to help people navigate large document collections. However, testing whether a topic model is good or not is notoriously hard, as it's subjective and requires asking real people about whether the outputs make sense. We show that you can ask a language model to recreate the answers of humans, correlating better with ground truth than previous evaluations.

title: Large Language Models Struggle to Describe the Haystack without Human Help: A Social Science-Inspired Evaluation of Large Research Language Models
summary: Large Language Models are increasingly used to help people understand document collections, but do they actually work better than traditional topic models? We tested how much users learn from LLM-generated topics versus traditional models and found that while LLMs produce more readable topics, they are often too generic for specialized domains. Adding human supervision helps, but traditional methods like LDA remain surprisingly effective: they just need better interfaces.

title: Topic models for decision-support systems, Part II: Expert-in-the-loop hierarchical topic models
summary: Topic models usually give you one flat list of topics, but sometimes you want different levels of detail—like seeing both "machine learning" and its subtopics "neural networks" or "reinforcement learning". Existing hierarchical topic models do this but are incredibly complex to tune. We introduce HTM-WS and HTM-DS, two methods that let experts build topic hierarchies interactively with minimal tuning, working with any topic model type, and we show they perform well on scientific datasets.

title: CASE: Large Scale Topic Exploitation for Decision Support Systems
summary: Topic models can help analyze large document collections, but they're rarely integrated into actual decision-making systems because it's hard to search and compute with them efficiently. CASE solves this by building on Solr search technology to enable fast semantic search and topic-based analysis at scale. We show how it works through two real applications: calculating science policy indicators and helping evaluate research project proposals.

title: Discrepancy Detection at the Data Level: Toward Consistent Multilingual Question Answering
summary: Multilingual question answering systems should give consistent answers across languages, but they need to distinguish between objective facts (like "What is jaundice?") and culturally-dependent questions (like "Who assists in childbirth?"). We introduce MIND, a user-in-the-loop pipeline that detects both factual errors and cultural discrepancies in multilingual QA systems, helping build systems that are both accurate and culturally aware.

title: ITMT: Interactive Topic Model Trainer
summary: Topic models are powerful but hard to use if you're not an NLP expert—you need to know how to tune parameters and compare different algorithms. We built ITMT, a graphical tool that lets domain experts train and refine topic models interactively without needing deep technical knowledge. It supports both classical and modern neural methods, making the whole process accessible to the people who actually understand the content.
